title: Osama bin Laden wasn't a poor boy who made good — he was the rich son of a Saudi royal builder
dek: Osama bin Laden was the 17th son of Mohammed bin Laden, drew hundreds of thousands of dollars a year in dividends as a child, and attended Jeddah's only elite day school — his radicalism was not a product of poverty but of privilege and Brotherhood recruitment.
why: Steve Coll uses family history to break ‘where do terrorists come from’ into verifiable detail: the rotating fourth wife, the PE teacher's after-school group, the 1979 Grand Mosque siege. High information density, but it takes a little patience.
who: Listeners interested in modern Middle Eastern history, the origins of terrorism, and how a family business binds itself to royal power; anyone who wants to understand the judgment that ‘radicals do not grow out of poverty.’
skip: The ad read from 24:15 to 25:16 can be skipped.

points.h: The elder bin Laden started out carrying sacks on the docks
points.body: Mohammed bin Laden came from Hadramawt in Yemen; as a boy of about ten he walked with his uncle to Jeddah, first worked as a dock porter, then learned bricklaying, then became a contractor. He lost an eye in a construction accident. His rise was bound up with Saudi Arabia itself: first the pilgrimage economy, then, after oil arrived in the 1930s, the royal family's building boom, which made him ‘the royal bricklayer.’ Steve Coll stresses that he was an outsider — no amount of money could make marrying his children into the royal family conceivable, just as a blue-blooded Northeastern American family would not marry its daughter to the Sicilian contractor who built its swimming pool.

points.h: The fourth wife was a rotating post
points.body: Mohammed bin Laden kept four wives at once; the first three were long-term fixtures, while the fourth slot was rapid marriage and rapid divorce, which Steve Coll says can only be described as his own sexual appetite. Osama's mother Aliyah was a 15-year-old girl from the Syrian coast, introduced to the elder bin Laden through a Syrian business deal, and about a year after Osama's birth she was passed on to a mid-level manager in the company. Osama was therefore ‘the child of a divorced wife,’ but he was also a ‘golden child’ — he held shares in this highly profitable company and drew hundreds of thousands of dollars a year in dividends in the 1960s and 70s.

points.h: Bin Laden boys grew up watching demolitions
points.body: The elder bin Laden's biggest project at the time was the modernisation of Mecca and Medina, which meant tearing down much of the old city. What the sons saw as teenagers was the daily routine of placing explosives in old buildings, stepping back, boom. Steve Coll says this cannot be causally connected to what Osama later became, but it is the true picture of their upbringing. At the same time the elder bin Laden was strict with his sons, repeatedly preaching simple living, hard work and study, and periodically summoning all his sons to company headquarters; daughters were not part of that gathering.

points.h: In 1967 his father died in a crash, and the eldest son Salem took over
points.body: Mohammed bin Laden's plane hit a mountainside; an American pilot judged it a landing error. The king wept, because the royal family was itself a debtor to the bin Laden organisation, and losing him meant all the construction projects would be thrown into disarray. The eldest son Salem was sent to London for his education, the only son sent to the West, and he loved the Beatles, played harmonica, flew private planes and threw global parties; he was described as a playboy and practical joker. He took over in his early twenties; European engineers kept the projects going, but every decision landed on him, including where Osama went to school and who could marry.

points.h: What changed him was a PE teacher's after-school group
points.body: Osama attended the elite day school in Jeddah founded by Irish and British educators, relatively secular. But there he was influenced by a Syrian PE teacher, a follower of the Muslim Brotherhood who ran after-school clubs and study groups for the children of elite families — the Brotherhood believed in gaining influence by recruiting and educating elites. Osama gradually became the family's ‘Puritan among Puritans’: no music, opposed to photographs, no modern plastic toothbrush, only a twig, and married for the first time at 17.

points.h: Among 54 siblings, he was the right-wing minority
points.body: Steve Coll likens Mohammed's 54 children to a parliament, divided between modern and traditional. The vast majority were globalists: properties in Europe and America, dancing in clubs, selling perfume in Geneva, running a Hard Rock Cafe in Beirut. The centrists tried to balance Saudi conservatism with the occasional trip abroad. Osama belonged to the family's right wing, with only a few siblings equally devout, and among them he became the leader and advocate, constantly reprimanding his siblings for what they said and did, and isolating himself in the process.

points.h: In a Saudi context, going to Pakistan was entirely normal
points.body: Steve Coll stresses that Osama volunteering in Saudi Arabia and on the Pakistan-Afghanistan border was in no way abnormal in a Saudi context — it was like a family of six children where one is more devout than his siblings and goes abroad through the church to help disaster victims build houses; the family would be proud of him, perhaps a little worried, but not opposed. Salem supported him too, giving him money and access. Only later, when he turned against his own family and the kingdom, did he cross the line. Throughout the 1980s, in our eyes, he was a supported, entirely conventional radical.

points.h: At the Mecca siege, the royals wanted the bin Laden family's blueprints
points.body: In 1979 hundreds of armed men seized the Grand Mosque in Mecca, their weapons smuggled in beforehand inside coffins, and the siege lasted two weeks. The militants hid in the basement, and the people who had the basement blueprints were the bin Laden family, then building the mosque, who were asked to help the special forces storming in. Osama, 22, watched it all on television. Steve Coll argues that what he learned was not the specific methods of this self-proclaimed Mahdi's group, but that a small group acting boldly in a public symbolic space can stir an entire society and attract the world's attention.

points.h: His real advantage was understanding media, not oratory
points.body: The Osama of the 1980s was consistently described as shy and soft-spoken, not a natural leader and not an orator. Steve Coll argues the key is that he grew up in a globalised business family with access to electronics and cutting-edge communications technology; he was trained as a marketer himself, and his sons worked in marketing in Jeddah. He was first a consumer of media, and later his own communicator. When he turned against his family and the kingdom and began exporting his own vision, he was extremely effective, because he mastered the tools of the day earlier than his contemporaries.
